A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Brain-IT and contain readable main text, figures, tables and appendices A-D. Retained content can be matched across pagination and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original fMRI reconstruction and transfer-learning results, including Table 1, component ablations and extensive qualitative reconstructions in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds clustering comparisons, a BIT-versus-MLP experiment, attention analyses and NSD-Synthetic reconstructions.

M1.justification: The voxel clustering, Brain Tokenizer, cross-transformer, semantic and VGG/DIP branches, training objectives and transfer procedure remain unchanged. The added statement that SDXL refinement uses no text prompt clarifies an existing step; the new clustering and MLP variants are experimental comparators.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation beyond NSD natural images to NSD-Synthetic stimuli, including geometric patterns and text stimuli, for Subject 1 (Appendix C.5, Fig. S7). This introduces a distinct out-of-distribution input domain. Existing NSD evaluation and COCO augmentation remain.

E2.justification: Table T2 adds Schaefer-400 and Schaefer-1000 parcellation comparators, while new Table T5 compares BIT against MLP predictors trained with InfoNCE and MSE losses. These directly test two central design choices. Table 1's comparator set is unchanged; the former 'Anatomical clustering' comparator is retained as '3D-coordinates clustering'.

E3.justification: Existing NSD splits, metrics, training budgets and transfer settings are unchanged. Added experiments introduce a Subject-1 MLP comparison, atlas configurations yielding 84 or 198 clusters, attention aggregation across layers and heads with spatial maps averaged over 1,000 test images, and NSD-Synthetic testing without adaptation.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis through the BIT-versus-MLP ablation, additional anatomical clustering controls, spatial and semantic token-selectivity analyses, and an out-of-distribution robustness test. These supplement the retained augmentation, cluster-count, branch-contribution, refinement and failure-case analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and subject averages without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. Averaging attention maps in v2 is part of the new analysis, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained numerical results are unchanged after matching renumbered tables. New Table T5 reports Subject-1 PixCorr of 0.500 for BIT, 0.267 for MLP-InfoNCE and 0.182 for MLP-MSE. Table T2 adds atlas results, with Schaefer-1000 exceeding functional clustering on Alex(2) and Incep. New attention and synthetic-stimulus figures add findings; Fig. S2 fills two missing NeuroVLA examples, while Figs. 3 and S3 change MindEye2/MindTuner attribution.

T1.justification: No formal assumptions, mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or revised. The new attention-map discussion describes empirical analyses of the existing architecture.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and discussion retain the same central claims: shared functional clusters, localized BIT predictions, complementary reconstruction branches and efficient transfer with limited recordings. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets attention patterns as evidence of contralateral spatial organization and semantic selectivity, and interprets NSD-Synthetic reconstructions as robust generalization. These extend the mechanism and applicability discussion. Existing explanations of branch complementarity, limitations and failure cases remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, a promise to release code, checkpoints and reconstructed images, and clarification that SDXL refinement uses no text prompt. It also documents the new comparators and attention aggregation. Appendix D's training, hardware and inference details are unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that the promised release occurred.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gifford et al. (2024) for NSD-Synthetic and Schaefer et al. (2018) for cortical parcellation. The related-work section and positioning relative to earlier reconstruction methods remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The existing narrative and main section order are largely retained. v2 locally revises Sections 3.1, 6 and A.2, adds explanations for the new appendix analyses and ethics/reproducibility statements, and updates author text and cross-references. There is little extensive rewriting of existing material.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial attention-map and cortical-map displays in Figs. S5-S6, synthetic-stimulus reconstructions in Fig. S7, and Table T5; Table T2 gains comparator rows. It also revises comparison labels and the BIT schematic, changes the author/header layout, and relocates retained appendix displays. The former branch and failure figures survive as Figs. S8-S9.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens support for the existing method through direct architecture and clustering controls, makes token behavior inspectable, and supplies previously missing comparison examples. The gains are useful but limited: the MLP comparison covers one subject, NSD-Synthetic evidence is qualitative and restricted to Subject 1, and semantic selectivity is illustrated through selected attention maps. The core results and reproducibility details remain largely unchanged, supporting a modest overall improvement.
